buttons: CSS Buttons: Sizes, Icons & Hover Effects
Choose filled buttons for primary actions, outlines for secondary actions and small buttons only where labels remain readable.
Use button for an action and an anchor for navigation. Give icon-only controls an accessible name.
Hover effects supplement the action label. Reduced-motion settings should preserve a clear static state.
cards: CSS Cards: Responsive Grids & Hover States
Group one subject per card, then combine cards with the grid utilities for product, feature or project collections.
Use a heading for each card and meaningful link text. Avoid nesting interactive controls inside a whole-card link.
Cards do not need JavaScript; fetching their content and filtering collections are application responsibilities.
forms: CSS Form Controls: Inputs, Labels & Selects
Use consistent fields for data entry and reserve helper text for instructions that readers need before submitting.
Associate every label with its control and connect errors with aria-describedby. Do not rely only on color for invalid fields.
Native selects remain usable without customizable-select support. Submission and server validation need application code.
accordions: CSS Accordion: Single & Multiple Open Panels
Use disclosures for secondary explanations and FAQs. Keep essential instructions visible outside collapsed content.
Retain details and summary so Enter and Space work natively. Give each independent exclusive group its own name.
The name attribute enables exclusive groups in supporting browsers. Smooth closing is progressive enhancement, not a requirement for reading the answer.
headers: Pick a logo/menu arrangement that fits your navigation, and keep the primary action easy to find on small screens.
Use a labelled navigation landmark, real links and the native Menu disclosure. Keep the current page identifiable.
Headers respond to their available container width. Test long translated labels and zoom rather than relying only on a device width.
footers: Use footer columns for secondary navigation, project resources and clear ownership information.
Give repeated navigation a distinguishing label and keep link contrast readable in both themes.
Footer grids can stack naturally on narrow screens; legal, support and contact copy must match your own project.
heroes: CSS Hero Sections: Layouts & Calls to Action
Lead with a specific benefit, a short explanation and a primary link to the next useful action.
Keep one page-level h1 and meaningful CTA text. Decorative illustrations should not compete with the reading order.
Hero layouts are CSS-only; avoid making the main heading depend on an animation completing.
links: CSS Links: Underlines, Icons & Hover Effects
Use underlines and deliberate spacing to make links recognizable within paragraphs and navigation.
Preserve a visible keyboard focus indicator and ensure icon decoration is not the only accessible name.
Hover is unavailable on many touch devices, so the destination and purpose must be clear before interaction.
sliders: CSS Sliders: Scroll Snap & Range Inputs
Choose a scroll-snap rail for a small collection that readers can browse at their own pace, or a range input for a numeric setting.
Label the scroll region and keep visible navigation links. Range inputs need an associated label and a meaningful value range.
These carousels do not autoplay or announce a scripted active slide. Dynamic synchronization belongs to an application integration.
editor: CSS WYSIWYG Editor Layout & Rich Text
Use the editor module for a rich-text canvas, wrapping toolbar and read-only document presentation.
Give the editable region a clear accessible label and keep formatting buttons named and keyboard reachable.
CSS styles the editor; formatting commands, sanitization, undo and saving are not supplied by this module.
tabs: CSS Tabs That Become Mobile Accordions
Use the responsive pattern when desktop readers benefit from side-by-side section choices and mobile readers need stacked disclosures.
The controls keep native details semantics. Do not add tablist roles unless you also implement their keyboard interaction model.
The same content is used at both widths. The layout changes at a 48rem container width; smooth height transitions depend on browser support.
testimonials: CSS Testimonials: Quote Cards, Grids & Sliders
Present real customer quotes with a clear attribution, and choose a grid when comparing several quotes matters.
Use blockquote and attribution markup, and let readers browse slider content without timed movement.
Example names and quotes are fictional. Replace them with permissioned testimonials before publishing.
grid: CSS Grid Layouts: Responsive Columns & Gaps
Use explicit columns when the layout has a known structure, or the auto grid when item widths should determine the column count.
Keep DOM order meaningful so keyboard and screen-reader order matches the intended reading sequence.
The base grid starts with one column; responsive classes add columns at their documented breakpoints.
flex: CSS Flexbox: Wrapping Rows & Sidebar Layouts
Use a cluster for wrapping rows of controls and the sidebar pattern for a flexible content region beside navigation.
Allow labels to wrap, preserve source order and avoid shrinking interactive targets below a usable size.
Test long labels and enlarged text. A layout that wraps naturally needs fewer device-specific overrides.
tables: Responsive CSS Tables & Mobile Data Rows
Use a table for real relationships between rows and columns. Add captions and choose stacked or scrollable presentation deliberately.
Use column headers and row labels, and preserve every field in the narrow-screen representation.
Stacked labels must match the headers. Dense data may be better served by an accessible horizontal scroll region.
feedback: Use alerts for relevant status information and badges for short categories or counts rather than full instructions.
Include text that explains the state. Select live-region behavior only when an application actually updates important information.
CSS controls presentation; asynchronous announcements and dismissal state need an appropriate application integration.
typography: CSS Typography: Fluid Headings & Text Rhythm
Use fluid headings to scale comfortably, and keep body copy at a readable size with a consistent text measure.
Keep the heading outline logical and allow browser text enlargement. Do not use heading tags only to get a visual size.
The framework uses a system font stack. The documentation website separately loads its branded fonts.
animations: CSS Animations: Scroll Reveals & Hover Motion
Use motion to clarify an interaction or draw attention to a meaningful change, not to hide essential information.
Respect reduced motion and keep controls usable by keyboard and touch. Content must remain readable without scroll-animation support.
Scroll-driven effects and advanced interpolation are progressive enhancements with browser-dependent support.
cursors: CSS Cursor Effects & Section Hover States
Apply cursor treatments sparingly to indicate an interactive surface while preserving native text and control cursors.
Keep ordinary focus styles and do not rely on a custom cursor as the only indication that something is clickable.
Coarse pointers and forced colors retain native behavior. Pointer-following trails require JavaScript and are not implemented here.
avatars: Use avatars to support identification in comments, teams and compact profile summaries.
Use a useful image alternative when the image adds identity, or empty alt text when an adjacent name provides it.
Status dots need accompanying text for important presence information; CSS cannot establish a user’s actual online state.
breadcrumbs: Use breadcrumbs to show a content hierarchy on documentation or category pages, with the current page at the end.
Label the breadcrumb navigation and apply aria-current to the current location. Keep separators decorative.
Breadcrumbs describe hierarchy rather than a browser back stack. Keep their destinations aligned with your real site structure.
pagination: CSS Pagination Links & Current Page States
Use pagination for collections with real page destinations, keeping the next and previous actions easy to locate.
Label the navigation and mark the current page. Give abbreviated or icon-only controls understandable names.
The examples style navigation; slicing records, fetching pages and updating the address belong to your application.
selection: Use checkboxes for independent choices, radios for a single choice and switches for an immediate on/off preference.
Keep the native input, associate its label and use a fieldset/legend for related choices.
CSS exposes checked and disabled states. Saving preferences or applying their effects is separate application behavior.
chips: Use chips to summarize categories, filters or short metadata, with a clear distinction between static and interactive items.
Do not make a static tag look like an unexplained button. Removal controls need a label naming what will be removed.
The examples provide styling and native selection patterns; collection updates require application state.
collections: Use a disclosure for a compact group of navigation links, and native select controls for a labelled selection task.
Retain standard link and input semantics. A custom menu role requires keyboard behavior beyond ordinary tab navigation.
These patterns do not claim a scripted ARIA menu or listbox implementation; use native controls when that behavior is needed.
text-fields: CSS Text Fields, Search, Number & OTP Inputs
Choose the native input type that matches the task, including email, search, number or a single verification-code field.
Provide persistent labels, autocomplete hints and instructions before a user makes an error.
Native validation is a convenience, not a security boundary. OTP sending and verification need backend logic.
form-patterns: CSS Form Layouts, Help Text & Error Messages
Group related fields and make the expected information clear before presenting validation feedback.
Use fieldset/legend for groups and aria-describedby for help and errors. Error text should identify a correction.
Form saving, server validation and success announcements belong to the application rather than the stylesheet.
pickers: Use a native datalist for a small static set of suggestions when free text is also acceptable.
Give the input a real label and explain whether suggestions are optional or a fixed set of allowed choices.
A datalist is not a complete ARIA combobox. Remote filtering, virtualized options and custom keyboard behavior need application code.
colors: CSS Color Controls: Pickers, Swatches & Sliders
Use a native color input for real color entry and labelled swatches for a small set of known palette choices.
Name each swatch so its meaning is available without seeing the color, and keep selected state distinguishable.
The two-dimensional gradient is illustrative. Slider-to-color conversion, synchronization and theme updates require application code.
dates: Prefer native date/time fields for reliable entry. Use the fixed-month calendar as an example of day-selection presentation.
Provide labels and format guidance. Explain date-range constraints and validation messages in text.
The sample calendar is fixed to October 2026. Month navigation, localization and range calculations are not implemented by CSS.
status: Choose progress for known completion, a meter for a measured value and a short loading indicator for unknown duration.
Label native progress and meter elements. Give important loading states readable text and avoid announcing every visual frame.
Progress values must reflect real application state. Reduced motion keeps loading decoration from continuous movement.
surfaces: Use surfaces to group related content and separators to clarify boundaries without adding unnecessary visual weight.
Name toolbar groups and preserve ordinary keyboard order unless you implement the composite toolbar interaction model.
Scroll shadows indicate additional content visually; keep the region scrollable and understandable without that effect.
keyboard: Use kbd markup to show an actual shortcut near the related action, with the platform convention your application supports.
Write a readable shortcut label and avoid replacing the control’s accessible name with only symbols.
The CSS only draws the hint. The application must implement and document the shortcut itself.
modals: CSS Modal Dialogs with Native HTML Commands
Use a modal for a focused task that needs a deliberate decision before returning to the underlying page.
Give the dialog a name, a visible close action and a sensible initial focus target. Verify Escape and focus return.
The examples use native dialog invoker commands in supporting browsers. Test your target browsers or provide an application fallback.
alert-dialogs: Reserve urgent confirmation dialogs for choices whose consequences need explicit explanation.
Use concise text, a clear cancel action and initial focus that does not accidentally encourage a destructive choice.
Showing the dialog is native in supported browsers; the confirmed operation must be implemented by your application.
drawers: Use a drawer for a focused secondary task or navigation area while keeping its purpose and close action clear.
When modal, preserve native dialog focus containment and a useful accessible name. Keep long content scrollable.
Native command support and discrete opening transitions vary across browsers; the panel must remain usable without the animation.
popovers: CSS Popovers with Native HTML Controls
Use a popover for brief supporting controls that can be dismissed without completing a blocking task.
Name the trigger and use native popovertarget behavior. Interactive content must remain keyboard reachable.
Popover placement and dismissal are native where supported. The example does not implement a full application menu interaction model.
tooltips: CSS Tooltips for Hover & Keyboard Focus
Use a tooltip only for short supporting information; keep essential meaning in the visible control or nearby text.
Ensure the trigger has a complete name. Test keyboard focus and avoid putting interactive controls inside a tooltip.
These CSS hints are not a complete scripted tooltip controller. Touch users still need the underlying information to be understandable.
toasts: Use a toast for brief nonblocking feedback and keep important errors available in persistent page content.
Choose announcements deliberately and make dismissal understandable. Do not remove important text before a user can read it.
The examples demonstrate presentation and native dismissal; queues, timers and live announcements need application logic.
component-reference: CSS Component Index & Native HTML Alternatives
Use the index to find the closest StyloftCSS example for each reference component family.
Follow the semantics in each linked example and read its integration notes before adding application roles or state.
Coverage is a mapping of examples and alternatives, not a claim of React API or behavior parity with another UI library.
